blurb: How qubits really work, what quantum computers can and can't do, and why fixing errors decides everything — from scratch.

steps.p: Every normal computer stores information as bits: each is either 0 or 1, like a light switch that's off or on.
A qubit can be in a blend of 0 and 1 at the same time — called superposition. Each option has an "amplitude" that sets how likely it is to show up.
steps.analogy: A spinning coin: it isn't heads or tails until it lands.

steps.p: When you look at a qubit, the blend vanishes and you get a plain 0 or 1, with odds set by the amplitudes. You never see the blend directly.
Describing n qubits takes 2ⁿ amplitudes. 50 qubits need about a quadrillion numbers — too many for normal computers to track.

visual.caption: Not to scale — the real gap is far bigger.

steps.p: Quantum algorithms arrange amplitudes so wrong answers cancel out and right answers reinforce, like waves meeting in water. Then measuring likely gives the right answer.
steps.analogy: Noise-cancelling headphones: waves that cancel make silence; waves that add make it louder.

cards.q: You measure a qubit that's in superposition. What do you get?
options: A single 0 or 1, with odds set by its amplitudes
cards.why: A plain 0 or 1. Measuring ends the blend. The skill is arranging things so the answer you want is the likely one.

cards.statement: A quantum computer speeds up any problem by trying all possible answers in parallel.
cards.why: False. Measuring gives just one random result. Speedups come only from problems where interference can steer toward the right answer.

cards.q: How many amplitudes does it take to describe the state of 50 qubits?
cards.why: 2⁵⁰ ≈ a quadrillion. Each extra qubit doubles the count. That explosion is why normal computers struggle to simulate quantum ones.

cards.title: Richard Feynman proposed quantum computers in 1981 to simulate nature — not to break codes.
cards.detail: He argued nature is quantum, so simulating it efficiently needs a quantum machine. The code-breaking angle arrived in 1994 with Peter Shor's algorithm.

cards.statement: Entangled qubits can be used to send messages faster than light.
cards.why: False. Measuring one shows a correlation with the other, but each result is random on its own. No message can be sent that way.

cards.title: Making a qubit in the real world

steps.p: Nobody knows the best way yet. Leading approaches include tiny superconducting circuits, single charged atoms (trapped ions), neutral atoms held by lasers, and particles of light.
Any heat, vibration or stray signal disturbs a qubit's delicate state. That loss is called decoherence.
steps.analogy: Like trying to keep a soap bubble perfect in a windy room.

steps.p: Superconducting chips are kept at about 0.01 degrees above absolute zero — colder than deep space — inside large chandelier-like fridges.
Qubits only stay coherent for a short time — microseconds to seconds depending on the type. All the computing has to finish first.
In 2019 Google claimed its chip did in 200 seconds what a supercomputer would need 10,000 years for. Better classical methods later narrowed that gap a lot.

cards.q: Roughly how cold are superconducting quantum chips kept?
options: About 0.01 K — colder than deep space
cards.why: About 0.01 K. Deep space is about 2.7 K. Extreme cold removes heat that would disturb the qubits.

options: A qubit losing its quantum state through contact with its surroundings
A qubit being deleted on purpose
cards.hint: The soap bubble in the wind.
cards.why: Losing the quantum state. The environment "measures" the qubit by accident, wiping out the blend the computation relies on.

cards.statement: Trapped-ion quantum computers use individual charged atoms held in place by electric fields.
cards.why: True. Each ion is a qubit, controlled with lasers. They're very accurate but tend to be slower than superconducting qubits.

cards.title: In 2019, Google said its Sycamore chip did in 200 seconds what a supercomputer would need 10,000 years for.
cards.detail: IBM disputed the estimate, arguing it would take days, and later classical methods narrowed the gap further. The task itself had no practical use.

cards.q: Which of these is NOT a leading way to build qubits today?
cards.why: Vacuum tubes. They powered 1940s computers but play no part in quantum computing.

steps.p: Shor's algorithm could factor huge numbers fast, breaking RSA — the encryption guarding much of the internet. It needs a large, error-corrected machine that doesn't exist yet.
Grover's algorithm searches unsorted data in about the square root of the steps: 1,000,000 items in about 1,000 tries.

visual.caption: Searching a million unsorted items (worst case).

steps.p: Feynman's original idea: chemistry is quantum, so quantum computers could model molecules for new drugs, batteries and fertilisers.
Attackers may store encrypted data now to decrypt later. So new "post-quantum" encryption is already being rolled out.
steps.analogy: Changing the locks before the master key is made.

steps.p: For most everyday tasks — email, games, spreadsheets — quantum computers offer no advantage at all.

cards.q: With Grover's algorithm, roughly how many steps to search 1,000,000 unsorted items?
cards.hint: The square root of a million.
cards.why: About 1,000. √1,000,000 = 1,000. Useful, but a square-root speedup — not exponential.

cards.statement: A powerful quantum computer would make all encryption useless.
cards.why: False. It would break some kinds (like RSA). Others, including new post-quantum standards, are believed to resist it.

cards.title: In 2024, the US standards body NIST published its first encryption standards designed to resist quantum computers.
cards.detail: They include ML-KEM for exchanging keys and ML-DSA for digital signatures, built on maths believed to withstand quantum attacks.

cards.q: What does "harvest now, decrypt later" refer to?
options: Attackers storing encrypted data today to decrypt once quantum computers are strong enough
cards.why: Steal now, read later. Secrets that must stay secret for decades need quantum-safe encryption today.

cards.statement: Grover's search algorithm gives an exponential speedup over normal search.
cards.hint: Look at the bars: square root, not exponential.
cards.why: False. It's a square-root speedup. Big, but much less dramatic than the exponential speedup Shor's algorithm gives for factoring.

lessons.title: Errors, hype and the road ahead

cards.title: Why fixing errors is the whole game

steps.p: Today's qubits make an error roughly once every few hundred to few thousand operations. Useful algorithms need billions of error-free steps.
Error correction stores one reliable "logical" qubit across many physical qubits, constantly checking for and fixing mistakes.
steps.analogy: Like saying an important number three times on a crackly phone line, so the listener can fix any one mistake.

steps.p: Error correction only helps if physical qubits are good enough. Recently, labs showed adding more qubits finally made logical qubits better, not worse.
Breaking 2048-bit RSA is estimated to need around a million physical qubits. Today's biggest machines have about a thousand.
Qubit counts alone mean little: quality, connectivity and error rates matter more. Several "impossible for supercomputers" claims were later matched by cleverer normal methods.

cards.q: By recent estimates, roughly how many physical qubits might it take to break 2048-bit RSA?
cards.why: Around a million. A 2025 estimate put it just under a million noisy qubits — far beyond today's machines.

cards.statement: A quantum computer with more qubits is always more powerful than one with fewer.
cards.why: False. A few high-quality, well-connected qubits can beat many noisy ones. Error rates matter as much as counts.

options: Spreads one reliable qubit across many noisy ones, fixing mistakes as they happen
Deletes wrong answers after the computation
Restarts the computer when it fails
cards.hint: Repeating a number on a crackly phone line.
cards.why: Redundancy plus checking. Many physical qubits work together so the information survives individual errors.

cards.title: Several "beyond any supercomputer" quantum results were later matched or approached by cleverer normal methods.
cards.detail: Better simulation techniques keep raising the bar, so claims of quantum advantage are now judged on whether the task is useful and whether classical methods have truly been beaten.

cards.q: What does NISQ, the name for today's era of quantum computing, stand for?
cards.why: Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum. Coined by physicist John Preskill in 2018: machines too noisy for full error correction but too big to simulate easily.

cards.title: Run quantum headlines through three questions
cards.body: Is the task useful? Have the best normal computers been tried? Were the qubits error-corrected?
cards.challenge: Next time you see a quantum computing headline, check it against those three questions.
